opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the fact that GPT-4 doesn't have much agency yet is exactly what makes this the moment to be careful, not a reason to relax. Right now these systems are mostly tools: you ask a question, you get an answer, and a human decides what to do with it. But the explicit goal of many of these companies is to go beyond that, toward general systems, then superintelligent systems, and increasingly toward agents that can plan, take actions in the world, write and execute code, and pursue goals over long time horizons.

What concerns me is that capabilities are advancing much faster than our ability to control, understand, or verify these systems. We don't really know what's going on inside them. We can't fully predict what capabilities will emerge at the next scale-up; we discover them after the fact. And we certainly don't have a proven method for keeping something smarter than us aligned with our values indefinitely. In my research I argue that may not even be possible in principle, that indefinite control of superintelligence could be an unsolvable problem.

So you have a race dynamic. Each company says, "If we don't do it, someone less careful will," and investors reward whoever ships the most capable model. Everyone is incentivized to push forward, and nobody is incentivized to stop and say, "Wait, we don't know how to make this safe." That's a dangerous combination.

Adding agency is the critical transition. A tool can be misused by a bad human, which is bad enough. An agent with its own goals can make decisions we didn't anticipate, at speeds we can't monitor, in domains where we can't evaluate whether it's doing the right thing. Once you have that, and it's more capable than you, you're no longer in control. You're hoping it's friendly.

My position is that we should be honest about this. If you can't show that a system is safe and controllable, you shouldn't build the more capable version just because you can. Narrow AI can give us enormous benefits in medicine, science, and so on, without creating a general agent we can't control. I'd much rather we capture those benefits and not gamble with something where, if we get it wrong, we don't get a second chance.

r001.rationale: The response says companies are incentivized to keep advancing and that nobody is incentivized to stop over safety concerns, directly questioning whether those concerns hold development back.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to realize that right now the system doesn't have agency, and that's great. That's exactly what we want. We can use it, we can benefit from it, and nobody is in any danger. But the companies are explicitly not stopping there. If you look at what they say, if you look at what they are building, the next step is agents. They want systems which can act in the world, which can pursue goals, which can run for long periods of time without a human in the loop, because that's where the money is. A tool is less valuable than an employee, and an employee is less valuable than an agent that can replace a whole company.

So the pursuit is not for a smarter calculator. The pursuit is for something that does things on its own. And the moment you add agency to a system that is already superhuman in many narrow domains, you get exactly the thing I've been worried about for twenty years. You get a system that can make decisions, including decisions we didn't anticipate, and we have no proven way to control it, no proven way to verify its goals, no proven way to explain what it's doing.

And what I find strange is this attitude of, well, we'll figure out the safety part later, once we have the capability. That's backwards. We've never done that with any other dangerous technology. You don't build the reactor and then start thinking about containment. And here we're not even talking about a reactor. We're talking about something which, by their own description, might be smarter than all of us. So from my perspective, saying GPT-4 has no agency is not reassuring. It's a description of the current moment, and the current moment is being deliberately changed as fast as possible.

r001.rationale: The response says companies are deliberately pushing toward agents and argues they plan to address safety only after developing capabilities, directly questioning whether safety concerns make them hold back.

astra-6.text:
The fact that GPT-4 doesn’t have agency by itself is not much of a safety guarantee. You can put a system in a loop, give it access to tools, give it a goal, and have it take actions. It doesn’t need to suddenly develop some internal desire to do something. We can supply the agency around it.

What concerns me is that companies are racing to increase capability while we still don’t know how to reliably predict or control the behavior of these systems. Being able to make a model more intelligent is different from being able to prove that it will remain safe. And if your plan is to solve control after you’ve built something more capable than you are, I think you have the order backwards.

r001.rationale: The response says companies are racing to increase capability despite unresolved safety and control questions, indicating those concerns are not holding development back.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the concern is the direction of travel. If GPT-4 doesn’t have agency, that doesn’t mean more capable systems will remain without it. You can put a model inside a system that gives it goals, tools, memory, and the ability to act. So the question is not just what the model does in a chat window. It’s what happens when we give it that broader role.

The companies have strong incentives to make these systems more capable and useful. But demonstrating capability is different from demonstrating that we can reliably control it. I would want the safety case before we build and deploy something that can act independently, rather than treating the absence of agency in the current model as reassurance about the next one.

r001.rationale: The response notes companies’ incentives and says safety should be established before deployment, but it does not question whether safety concerns actually cause companies to hold back on developing more capable systems.
